title: Combining dynamic head pose-gaze mapping with the robot conversational state for attention recognition in human-robot interactions

fields.value: Technical/experimental: the authors propose a dynamic Bayesian (IO-HMM) model for visual focus of attention recognition and evaluate it experimentally on the Vernissage dataset.

quotes.text: Experiments on a public dataset where the humanoid robot NAO plays the role of an art guide and quiz master demonstrate the benefit of the two contributions.

fields.value: Art exhibition (vernissage) guide scenario with the NAO robot, using a recorded dataset of natural interactions realized with a Wizard of Oz approach.

quotes.text: To illustrate the above, the main robotic setup which we have considered is based on the Vernissage scenario shown in Fig. 1.
It contains 10 natural interactions with a humanoid robot ”Nao”, realized using a Wizard of Oz approach.

fields.value: 14 persons (about 140 minutes of data) were retained for the experiments, drawn from the Vernissage dataset of 10 interactions.

quotes.text: Ultimately, this resulted in a dataset of 14 persons, amounting to around 140 minutes of data for our experiments.
It contains 10 natural interactions with a humanoid robot ”Nao”, realized using a Wizard of Oz approach.

fields.value: Nao first engages with the participants and explains three paintings (about 10 minutes per recording on average), then gives the participants a quiz in which they can discuss before answering.

quotes.text: In each recording (10 minutes on average), Nao first engages with the participants and explains them three paintings.
Then, he gives them a quiz in which participants can discuss before the person to whom a question was addressed gives the answer.

fields.value: Two human participants and one robot (NAO) per interaction session.

quotes.text: Each interaction involves two participants standing in front of Nao and free to walk around and look at different objects.
Experiments on a public dataset where the humanoid robot NAO plays the role of an art guide and quiz master demonstrate the benefit of the two contributions.

fields.value: Frame-based Recognition Rate (percentage of frames with correctly recognized VFOA), with ground truth from annotations and a Vicon motion capture system for head poses and gaze directions.

quotes.text: As performance measure we use “Frame based Recognition Rate (FRR)” which corresponds to the percentage of frames during which the VFOA has been correctly recognized.
In addition, a Vicon motion capturing system was deployed, with markers placed on the participant’s heads (they are visible in Fig. 8a), Nao’s head, and near painting locations.

fields.value: The dynamic midline model G2 was the best dynamic model, with an average gain of about 13% over the geometric baseline on Vicon head poses (66.6% vs 53.8% full). Using all context cues with G2 reached 72.6% on Vicon data.

quotes.text: Among the different dynamic models, G2 which implements the midline model is the best, leading to an average gain of 13% over the baseline.
Altogether, the use of all context cues brings a considerable improvement of more than 10%.

fields.value: Visual focus of attention (VFOA) of people, i.e. what or whom a person is looking at, recognized from head pose.

quotes.text: The ability to recognize the Visual Focus of Attention (VFOA, i.e. what or whom a person is looking at) of people is important for robots or conversational agents interacting with multiple people

fields.value: The authors define VFOA as what or whom a person is looking at, and frame the goal as monitoring people's visual attention relying on head pose.

quotes.text: Our objective is to monitor the visual attention of people in a given environment relying on head pose.

fields.value: VFOA recognition is described as playing a key role in turn-taking, engagement, intention monitoring, and identifying the addressee in multi-person interaction.

quotes.text: plays a key role in turn-taking, engagement or intention monitoring.
gaze is a good indicator of the addressee (to whom a person is speaking) which is an important information to know for robots or ECAs interacting with multiple people.

fields.value: An Input-Output HMM decodes VFOA from head pose, using dynamic gaze-to-head mapping models and robot dialog context (speaking state, addressee, topic). Head poses come from Vicon or a particle filter tracker on the NAO camera view.

quotes.text: We build our VFOA recognition model based on the HMM illustrated in the middle part of Figure 2, without exploiting the context at this stage.

As input head poses, we used both poses derived from the Vicon system and pose estimates obtained by applying to Nao’s camera view (see above) a particle filter tracker performing the joint head tracking and pose estimation with appearance head pose modeling (Khalidov and Odobez, 2013).

fields.value: Humanoid robot NAO, with a camera in its head used for head pose estimation and an art-guide/quiz-master role.

quotes.text: Experiments on a public dataset where the humanoid robot NAO plays the role of an art guide and quiz master demonstrate the benefit of the two contributions.
It contains 10 natural interactions with a humanoid robot ”Nao”, realized using a Wizard of Oz approach.

fields.value: Because NAO's head rotates over time, the camera view changes, so head poses had to be transformed into the camera's time-dependent coordinate system.

quotes.text: which is time-dependent since Nao sometimes rotates its head.

fields.value: The paper proposes a dynamic head-pose-to-gaze mapping and a robot dialog-context prior to improve recognition of people's visual focus of attention in a NAO art-guide scenario with two participants. On a 14-person dataset, the dynamic mapping and context together raised recognition accuracy substantially over a geometric baseline. The work addresses human attention recognition rather than measuring effects of the robot's own gaze.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ4; RQ5 — The paper defines VFOA (RQ1), uses the robot's conversational context such as addressee and speaking state to recognize attention in multiparty interaction (RQ2), implements head-pose-based VFOA recognition with gaze models (RQ4), and uses a NAO humanoid (RQ5). It does not measure effects of attention on people (RQ3) or how embodiment influences the study (RQ6).
